videos.title: My Horse Loves Jumping, But I Need More Brakes…
videos.description:
"My horse loves jumping, but I need more brakes."
It's a phrase many riders will recognise.
In this video, I share some thoughts inspired by a guest article from Dr James Cooling, founder of the Association of Professional Bit and Bridle Fitters.
When a horse becomes strong, rushes fences or feels difficult to stop, it's easy to assume we know why. But what if becoming strong is simply an observation rather than an explanation?
The article explores why it can be valuable to look beyond the behaviour and consider factors such as comfort, training, balance, fitness and how the horse experiences their equipment.

Read the article: https://www.thehorsephysio.co.uk/pages/blog?p=horse-strong-when-jumping

Find the Assocation of Professional Bit and Bridle Fitters here: https://apbbf.com

I'd love to hear your thoughts.
Do you use the same bit and bridle for jumping as you do for flatwork?
Or do you make changes depending on the activity?

videos.title: Climbing Snowdon Slowly | What The Mountain Taught Me About Listening To The Body
videos.description:
Yesterday I climbed Yr Wyddfa (Snowdon) — slowly, emotionally, and one step at a time. You can read my blog here:
https://www.thehorsephysio.co.uk/pages/blog?p=climbing-snowdon-slowly

This video is not really about climbing a mountain. It’s about slowing down, listening to the body, accepting support, and recognising that progress does not need to look impressive to matter.

If you enjoy reflections like this on horses, health, behaviour, well-being, and the connection between horse and human, you are very welcome to join my newsletter community here:
https://mailchi.mp/thehorsephysio/newsletter

In this video, I talk about:
* nearly giving up three times
* the encouragement of family and strangers
* pacing and recovery
* “the body whispers before it shouts”
* gratitude for the human body
* and what the mountain unexpectedly taught me about my own work as a physiotherapist

videos.title: How to stay safe around horses - without living in fear
videos.description:
How do you stay safe around horses—without becoming anxious or overly cautious?

In this video, I share a quieter, more thoughtful approach to horse safety - one that focuses on awareness, connection, and understanding, rather than control.

Drawing on my experience as a Chartered Physiotherapist, and insights from the Ridden Horse Pain Ethogram developed by Dr Sue Dyson and colleagues, I explore how behaviour is often a form of communication—and how subtle changes can matter more than we think.

This is not about eliminating risk completely.
It’s about recognising it earlier… and responding with curiosity rather than assumption.

If you’d like a simple place to begin, you can download my calm safety checklist here:

https://mailchi.mp/thehorsephysio/how-to-stay-safe-around-horses

In this video:
Why horse behaviour isn’t random
How discomfort can influence behaviour
The role of awareness in safety
What to notice in everyday interactions
A calmer, more connected approach to staying safe

About Sue Palmer, The Horse Physio
Chartered Physiotherapist supporting horses and humans
Helping you understand the link between behaviour, comfort, and performance

If you’d like more reflections like this, you’re very welcome to subscribe.

evidence.title: My Horse Loves Jumping, But I Need More Brakes…
evidence.text:
标题：My Horse Loves Jumping, But I Need More Brakes…
简介："My horse loves jumping, but I need more brakes."
It's a phrase many riders will recognise.
In this video, I share some thoughts inspired by a guest article from Dr James Cooling, founder of the Association of Professional Bit and Bridle Fitters.
When a horse becomes strong, rushes fences or feels difficult to stop, it's easy to assume we know why. But what if becoming strong is simply an observation rather than an explanation?
The article explores why it can be valuable to look beyond the behaviour and consider factors such as comfort, training, balance, fitness and how the horse experiences their equipment.

Read the article: https://www.thehorsephysio.co.uk/pages/blog?p=horse-strong-when-jumping

Find the Assocation of Professional Bit and Bridle Fitters here: https://apbbf.com

I'd love to hear your thoughts.
Do you use the same bit and bridle for jumping as you do for flatwork?
Or do you make changes depending on the activity?

Sue specialises in understanding the links between equine pain and behaviour, with a focus on prevention, partnership, and performance. She champions the kind and fair treatment of horses through empathetic education. Sue is registered with RAMP, ACPAT, IHA, CSP, and HCPC.
